segments.expected: "Nobody claims it," said the Clerk, answering herself. "As of twenty-five minutes to seven this morning, by a line on the harbour pump house's fault paper in the Proprietor's own hand, witnessed, which I have in my press. The warrant pays no share on red. Write that, please. No share paid. No claim. Held."

segments.expected: "Wrong," he said. "By my hand, once: the ache from sixteen past to twenty-two past, when the pumps kept Mr. Halden's count because we'd asked him to hold them. segments.expected: "Good." He stood up, slowly, with his bag. "Now there's a girl at the pump house with a hand starved white to the wrist on a cell, your aunt says, and she sent for me half an hour ago, and I've been here." segments.expected: "I'll not say that's my fault," she said. "I said it on Sunday. I'll not say it twice, because it's not a thing that gets truer for saying." She looked at the cases. "I'll not say it's yours either. I'll say I watched her do it right this morning from a crate, and every hand on that mud knew who'd taught her to wait for the price, and it wasn't me and it wasn't you. It was a healer and a girl's own sense." She was quiet. "I'd liked to have taught you that. I didn't know it."

segments.expected: "Then don't know." Mara took her hand away. "I sealed a page for you once so that nobody could say you'd borrowed a thing. We broke the seal on Sunday, you and I, both hands. It's done. It's in the Board's press with the morning, and with three accounts of three people counting, and nobody's drawn a line." She stood up. "That's the right place for it. I'll not ask you anything about it ever again, and I'll mean it."
